triples.rationale: Eliphaz says that those who sow improper things perish by the Lord's command and the breath of His anger. The letter says the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of His mouth. Both employ the Lord's breath as the means of overthrow, but Eliphaz's claim is not a verdict that Job is guilty, nor are his unnamed offenders identified with the letter's lawless one.
triples.source_text: By the Lord’s command they will perish; by the breath of His anger they will disappear.

target_units.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of His mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of His coming.

triples.relationship: Audible speech without a visible form
triples.rationale: Eliphaz reports hearing a breeze and a voice while seeing no form and not recognizing the presence. Deuteronomy recalls Israel hearing words but seeing no likeness at Horeb, only a voice. The shared feature is heard speech without a visible form; Deuteronomy explicitly names the Lord as speaker, and that identity or authority is not transferred to Eliphaz's unrecognized presence.

triples.relationship: Righteous benefit contrasted with the loss of the impious
triples.rationale: Eliphaz's account moves from fools' ruined way of life to the righteous eating gathered goods. Proverbs explicitly says that the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous. Both place the righteous person's benefit beside wrongdoing's loss. The source's pronouns are not used to identify particular owners or a transaction, and the proverb does not identify Job's lost property or endorse Eliphaz's application to him.

triples.relationship: Lament over help remaining far away
triples.rationale: Job contrasts his trust with help being far from him. The psalm directly asks the Lord not to put the speaker's help far away and to attend to his support. Both express distress through the distance of help, with Job stating his experienced lack and the psalm petitioning against it; the psalm's later claim that God heard the petition is not inserted into Job's present complaint.
triples.source_text: Had I not trusted in Him? But help is far from me.

target_units.text: But Thou, Lord, do not put my help far away; attend to my support.

triples.relationship: Petition for relief before departure from life
triples.rationale: Job asks for his wrongdoing to be forgotten and his sin cleansed before he departs into the earth and is no more. The psalm asks the Lord to hear and grant relief before the speaker departs and no longer exists. Both make anticipated departure the urgent setting for a petition, while Job's request for cleansing and the psalm's request for refreshment remain distinct.

triples.rationale: Job asks who grew hard against the mighty God and endured. Romans voices an imagined objection asking who has resisted God's purpose, then challenges a human being's answering back to God. Both formulate divine-human resistance as a rhetorical question. Job's complaint and Paul's reply to an objector are different arguments; neither identifies Job with Pharaoh or endorses every inference of the other speaker.

triples.relationship: Darkness and the land of the dead in lament
triples.rationale: Job describes the land to which he expects to go as without brightness or sight of mortal life. The psalm asks whether mercy is recounted in the grave or wonders known in darkness and a forgotten land. Both laments associate death with a dark land cut off from ordinary living experience; the comparison preserves their lamenting voices and does not construct a complete account of the afterlife.

triples.rationale: Job asks who could rebuild what God throws down or open what He shuts. In Isaiah the Lord declares that no one rescues from His hands and asks who will turn back His action. Both deny a human capacity to undo God's act. Isaiah does not supply Job's particular demolition or confinement images, and no specific prisoner or destroyed building is identified.
triples.source_text: If He throws down, who will build? If He shuts people in, who will open?

triples.relationship: Wind-carried leaves as an image of vulnerability
triples.rationale: Job asks why God would oppose one as frail as a wind-moved leaf or grass carried by a breeze. Isaiah's communal confession depicts people falling like leaves and being carried off by wind because of their lawless deeds. The shared plant-and-wind image expresses vulnerability, while the confession's stated guilt is not imposed on Job's plea.
